sentences.t:
Ðā cōm of mōre under misthleoþum
Grendel gongan, Godes yrre bær;
sentences.l: Then came from the moor, under the mist-slopes, Grendel walking; God’s anger he bore;
sentences.n: ‘Ðā cōm … Grendel gongan’ is ‘then Grendel came walking’: ‘cōm’ is the past of ‘cuman’ and takes the infinitive ‘gongan’, ‘to go, walk’, which says how he came; the subject ‘Grendel’ stands after both, as it often does when someone arrives. ‘of mōre under misthleoþum’ is ‘from the moor, under the mist-slopes’: ‘mōre’ is a dative singular after ‘of’, and ‘misthleoþum’ is a dative plural after ‘under’, from a neuter plural ‘hleoþu’, ‘slopes’ (the singular is ‘hlið’), so the picture is of mist lying on the hillsides. ‘Godes yrre bær’ is ‘bore God’s anger’: ‘yrre’ is a neuter noun, ‘anger’, the object of ‘bær’, the past of ‘beran’. The poet has already told us that Grendel descends from Cain and is under God’s ban, and this clause says it again as he walks in. The fitt begins here with a capital ‘Ð’ and a new scene.
sentences.i: Then Grendel came walking from the moor, under the misty slopes; he bore God’s anger.

sentences.t:
mynte se mānscaða manna cynnes
sumne besyrwan in sele þām hēan.
sentences.l: Meant the crime-scather a certain one of the kin of men to ensnare in the hall, the high one.
sentences.n: ‘mynte’ is the past of ‘myntan’, ‘intend, purpose’, with the infinitive ‘besyrwan’, ‘to ensnare, plot against’ (the root is ‘searu’, ‘cunning’). The subject ‘se mānscaða’ follows the verb. ‘mānscaða’ is a compound of ‘mān’, ‘crime, wickedness’, and ‘scaða’, ‘harmer, enemy’; I call it ‘crime-scather’ in the literal line and ‘wicked marauder’ in the idiomatic one, and the same ‘scaþa’ is in ‘hearmscaþa’ (766) and in ‘scynscaþa’ (707). ‘sumne’ is accusative masculine, ‘a certain one’, and ‘manna cynnes’ is a genitive that says which group he is one of, ‘of the kin of men’. ‘in sele þām hēan’ is ‘in the high hall’: ‘sele’ is a dative singular, ‘þām’ the dative of ‘se’, and ‘hēan’ the weak dative of ‘hēah’, ‘high’; Heorot is meant. ‘mynte’ comes again at 731 and 762; I give it ‘meant’ in the literal line and ‘intended’ in the idiomatic one.
sentences.i: The wicked marauder intended to ensnare one of mankind in that high hall.

sentences.t:
Wōd under wolcnum tō þæs þe hē wīnreced,
goldsele gumena gearwost wisse
fǣttum fāhne.
sentences.l: Strode under the clouds, until he the wine-hall, the gold-hall of men, most readily knew, gleaming with plates.
sentences.n: ‘Wōd’ is the past of ‘wadan’, ‘go, stride’, the verb behind English ‘wade’; ‘under wolcnum’ is ‘under the clouds’, a dative plural. ‘tō þæs þe’ is ‘until’, literally ‘to that which’, and the clause it opens ends in ‘wisse’, the past of ‘witan’, ‘know’, with the superlative adverb ‘gearwost’, ‘most readily, most clearly’; so ‘he knew the hall most clearly’ is ‘he could make it out plainly’. ‘wīnreced’ and ‘goldsele gumena’ are two names for the hall, both objects of ‘wisse’: ‘wīn’ is the drink of feasting, so ‘wine-hall’; ‘gold-hall’ is a ‘sele’, ‘hall’, adorned with gold; and ‘gumena’ is a genitive plural, ‘of men’. ‘fǣttum fāhne’ is ‘gleaming with plates’: ‘fǣttum’ is a dative plural of ‘fǣt’, ‘plate, sheet’ (of gold, I take it), and ‘fāhne’ is accusative masculine, so it agrees with ‘goldsele’ (a masculine noun) and not with the neuter ‘wīnreced’. ‘fāh’ can mean ‘gleaming, many-coloured’, but the same word also means ‘stained’ and ‘hostile’ (it is ‘gore-stained’ in ‘drēorfāh’ at 485), and I choose ‘gleaming’ because of the plates; I take that to be right, but the choice is mine.
sentences.i: He strode on under the clouds until he could see most plainly the wine-hall, the gold-hall of men, bright with its plates of gold.

sentences.t:
Ne wæs þæt forma sīð,
þæt hē Hrōþgāres hām gesōhte;
sentences.l: Not was that the first time, that he Hrothgar’s home sought out;
sentences.n: ‘Ne wæs þæt forma sīð’ is ‘that was not the first time’: ‘forma’ is ‘first’, and ‘sīð’ is ‘journey’, so ‘occasion’. The ‘þæt’ clause then says what ‘that’ was: ‘þæt hē Hrōþgāres hām gesōhte’, ‘that he sought out Hrothgar’s home’, with ‘hām’ an accusative and ‘gesōhte’ the past of ‘gesēcan’, ‘seek out, visit’ (the form does not tell indicative from subjunctive). The poet is recalling the twelve winters of Grendel’s raiding, told in the second fitt, so the English past perfect, ‘had sought out’, is the idiomatic way to put it.
sentences.i: It was not the first time that he had sought out Hrothgar’s home;

sentences.t:
nǣfre hē on aldordagum ǣr nē siþðan
heardran hǣle, healðegnas fand!
sentences.l: Never did he in life-days, before nor since, with harder luck hall-thanes find!
sentences.n: ‘nǣfre … ǣr nē siþðan’ is ‘never … before nor since’, and ‘on aldordagum’ is ‘in life-days’, a dative plural from ‘aldor’, ‘life, age’ (a different word from ‘aldor’, ‘lord’), meaning ‘in all his days’. ‘fand’ is the past of ‘findan’, ‘find’, and ‘healðegnas’ is its object, an accusative plural, ‘hall-thanes’: the retainers who serve in the hall (a ‘healðegn’ was rendered ‘hall-thane’ in the second fitt). The hard words are ‘heardran hǣle’. I take ‘heardran’ as the comparative ‘harder’ and ‘hǣle’ as a dative of ‘hǣl’, ‘luck, omen, good fortune’, giving ‘with harder luck’, so that the clause says that Grendel never met worse luck than this among hall-thanes; that is a guess. The apparatus shows the line was a puzzle: editors read ‘hilde’ (‘battle’), ‘hæle[ðas]’ (‘heroes’), ‘hæle[scipes]’, or ‘hwīle’ or ‘mǣle’ (‘time’), and one reads ‘helðegn onfand’ for the end of the line, so the sense I give is Klaeber’s printing read as plainly as the grammar allows. The exclamation mark is Klaeber’s.
sentences.i: Never in all his days, before or since, did he find, to his harder luck, hall-thanes!

sentences.t:
Cōm þā tō recede rinc sīðian
drēamum bedǣled.
sentences.l: Came then to the hall the warrior journeying, of joys deprived.
sentences.n: ‘Cōm þā tō recede rinc sīðian’ is ‘then the warrior came to the hall, journeying’: ‘cōm’ takes the infinitive ‘sīðian’, ‘to journey’, and ‘rinc’ is the subject, ‘man, warrior’, a word that normally means a fighting man and is here used of Grendel. ‘drēamum bedǣled’ is ‘deprived of joys’: ‘bedǣled’ is the past participle of ‘bedǣlan’, ‘deprive’, nominative masculine, agreeing with ‘rinc’, and the verb takes a dative of what is lost, ‘drēamum’, ‘joys’ (the plural of ‘drēam’, ‘joy, revelry’). The poet has made Grendel an exile from joy in the earlier fitts.
sentences.i: Then the warrior came journeying to the hall, robbed of joy.

sentences.t:
Duru sōna onarn
fȳrbendum fæst, syþðan hē hire folmum (æthr)ān;
sentences.l: The door at once ran open, fast with fire-bands, as soon as he touched it with his hands;
sentences.n: ‘Duru’ is a feminine noun, ‘door’, the subject of ‘onarn’, the past of ‘onirnan’, ‘run open, spring open’. ‘fȳrbendum fæst’ is ‘fast with fire-bands’: ‘fæst’ is ‘fixed, fastened’, and ‘fȳrbendum’ is a dative plural of a compound of ‘fȳr’, ‘fire’, and ‘bend’, ‘band’; I take it as bands forged in fire, which is a guess, and at 774 the hall as a whole is bound with ‘īrenbendum’, ‘iron bands’. ‘syþðan hē hire folmum (æthr)ān’ is ‘as soon as he touched it with his hands’: ‘syþðan’ with a past tense means ‘as soon as’; ‘hire’ is a feminine dative, ‘it’, because ‘duru’ is feminine, and ‘æthrān’, the past of ‘æthrīnan’, ‘touch’, takes a dative; ‘folmum’ is a dative plural of ‘folm’, ‘hand’. The parentheses show that the manuscript is damaged here: the packet’s apparatus gives its reading as some lost letters and then ‘(hr)an’, and Klaeber supplies ‘æthr’. Other editors supply ‘gehr’ or only ‘hr’, giving ‘gehrān’ or ‘hrān’; all of them mean ‘touched’, so the sense is the same whichever letters are lost.
sentences.i: The door, fastened with bands forged in fire, sprang open at once, as soon as his hands touched it;

sentences.t:
onbrǣd þā bealohȳdig, ðā (hē ge)bolgen wæs,
recedes mūþan.
sentences.l: Wrenched open then the bale-minded one, when he enraged was, the hall’s mouth.
sentences.n: ‘onbrǣd’ is the past of ‘onbregdan’, ‘pull open, wrench open’, and its object comes last, ‘recedes mūþan’, ‘the hall’s mouth’: ‘mūþan’ is an accusative singular (‘mūþa’ is a weak masculine noun, ‘mouth’), and the ‘mouth’ of a building is its doorway. ‘bealohȳdig’ is a nominative adjective, ‘bale-minded’, from ‘bealu’, ‘harm, evil’, and ‘-hȳdig’, ‘-minded’ (the root is ‘hyge’, ‘mind’); it is a noun-like epithet for Grendel, ‘the one intent on harm’. ‘ðā (hē ge)bolgen wæs’ is ‘when he was enraged’: ‘gebolgen’ is the past participle of ‘belgan’, ‘be angry’, and ‘wæs gebolgen’ is the state. The parentheses mark letters lost to the fire: the manuscript keeps only ‘bolgen’, and Klaeber, following Zupitza and others, supplies ‘hē ge’; Kemble and others read ‘hē ā’, giving ‘ābolgen’, which means the same.
sentences.i: Then, in his rage, the one bent on harm tore open the mouth of the hall.

sentences.l: Quickly after that onto the gleaming floor the fiend trod, went wrathful-minded;
sentences.n: ‘Raþe æfter þon’ is ‘quickly after that’: ‘raþe’ is an adverb and ‘þon’ an instrumental form, ‘after that’. ‘on fāgne flōr’ is ‘onto the gleaming floor’: ‘on’ with the accusative gives motion, ‘flōr’ is masculine, and ‘fāgne’ is accusative masculine of ‘fāh’, the same word as ‘fāhne’ at 716, with the stem spelled ‘fāg-’ before an ending; the floor is patterned or gleaming, so ‘gleaming, variegated’ is the sense I take. ‘fēond’ is ‘foe, fiend’ and the subject; ‘treddode’ is the past of ‘treddian’, ‘tread’. ‘ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’, ‘go’, an irregular verb, and ‘yrremōd’ is a nominative adjective, ‘wrathful-minded’, from ‘yrre’, ‘anger’, and ‘mōd’, ‘mind’.
sentences.i: Quickly after that the fiend trod onto the gleaming floor and went on, wrathful;

sentences.t:
him of ēagum stōd
ligge gelīcost lēoht unfǣger.
sentences.l: from him out of eyes stood, most like to fire, a light unlovely.
sentences.n: ‘him of ēagum stōd’ is ‘from his eyes stood’: ‘him’ is a dative that tells whose eyes (a possessive dative), ‘ēagum’ is a dative plural after ‘of’, ‘out of’, and ‘stōd’ is the past of ‘standan’, here ‘stood forth, shone’. The subject comes last, ‘lēoht unfǣger’, ‘a light unlovely’: ‘lēoht’ is a neuter noun, and ‘unfǣger’ is ‘un-’ with ‘fǣger’, ‘fair’, so ‘not fair, ugly’. ‘ligge gelīcost’ is ‘most like to fire’: ‘gelīcost’ is the superlative of ‘gelīc’, ‘like’, and it takes a dative, ‘ligge’, the dative of ‘līg’, ‘flame’, spelled with a double ‘g’ here.
sentences.i: A light stood out from his eyes, most like fire, and ugly.

sentences.t:
Geseah hē in recede rinca manige,
swefan sibbegedriht samod ætgædere,
magorinca hēap.
sentences.l: He saw in the hall many of warriors sleeping, the kin-band, together at once, the troop of young-warriors.
sentences.n: ‘Geseah’ is the past of ‘gesēon’, ‘see’. ‘rinca manige’ is ‘many warriors’: ‘manige’ is an accusative plural, ‘many’, and ‘rinca’ is a genitive plural, ‘of warriors’, so ‘many of warriors’. ‘swefan’ is the infinitive of ‘swefan’, ‘sleep’, after ‘geseah’: ‘saw … sleep’. ‘sibbegedriht’ and ‘magorinca hēap’ then name the same men again, in the accusative: ‘sibbegedriht’ is a feminine noun, ‘band of kinsmen’, ‘kin-band’ (as in fitt VI), and ‘magorinca’ is a genitive plural, ‘of young warriors’, from ‘magu’, ‘boy, young man’, and ‘rinc’, ‘warrior’, with ‘hēap’, ‘troop’, an accusative singular. ‘samod ætgædere’ is ‘together’, two adverbs with the same meaning set side by side for emphasis. Two editors print ‘sibb-’ for ‘sibbe-’, which makes the word a syllable shorter and means the same.
sentences.i: He saw in the hall many warriors asleep, a band of kinsmen all together, a troop of young fighters.

sentences.t: Þā his mōd āhlōg;
sentences.l: Then his mind laughed out;
sentences.n: ‘āhlōg’ is the past of ‘āhliehhan’, ‘laugh out, exult’, with ‘his mōd’, ‘his mind, his spirit’, as subject: the laugh is Grendel’s gloating, not mirth. ‘Þā’ is ‘then’. The unit is one short clause that Klaeber closes with a semicolon.
sentences.i: Then his heart exulted;

sentences.t:
mynte þæt hē gedǣlde, ǣr þon dæg cwōme,
atol āglǣca ānra gehwylces
līf wið līce, þā him ālumpen wæs
wistfylle wēn.
sentences.l: He meant that he would part, ere day should come, the terrible awesome one, of each one life from body, since to him had befallen hope of a feast’s-fill.
sentences.n: ‘mynte þæt hē gedǣlde’ is ‘he meant that he would part’: ‘gedǣlde’ is the past of ‘gedǣlan’, ‘divide, separate’, and the verb takes ‘līf wið līce’, ‘life from body’ (‘wið’ with the dative ‘līce’ is ‘apart from’), with ‘ānra gehwylces’, a genitive, ‘of each one’, saying whose life. ‘ǣr þon dæg cwōme’ is ‘before day came’: ‘ǣr þon’ is ‘before’, and ‘cwōme’ is a past subjunctive of ‘cuman’ (the indicative is ‘cwōm’, so the ending ‘-e’ marks the subjunctive). ‘atol āglǣca’ is ‘the terrible awesome one’ and is in apposition to ‘hē’; ‘āglǣca’ is a disputed word for a fierce opponent, which I render ‘awesome one’ throughout, as in fitt II. ‘þā him ālumpen wæs wistfylle wēn’ is ‘since the hope of a full meal had befallen him’: ‘ālumpen’ is the past participle of ‘ālimpan’, ‘befall’, ‘wēn’ is a feminine noun, ‘hope, expectation’, and ‘wistfylle’ is a genitive, ‘of a feast’s-fill’ (‘wist’, ‘food’, and ‘fyllu’, ‘fill’). ‘þā’ could be ‘when’ or ‘since’; ‘since’ gives the reason for his gloating.
sentences.i: The terrible awesome one meant to sever, before day came, the life from the body of every one of them, for the hope of a full meal had come to him.

sentences.t:
Ne wæs þæt wyrd þā gēn,
þæt hē mā mōste manna cynnes
ðicgean ofer þā niht.
sentences.l: Not was that fate any longer, that he more might of the kin of men partake beyond that night.
sentences.n: ‘Ne wæs þæt wyrd þā gēn’ is ‘that was not fate any longer’: ‘wyrd’ is a feminine noun, ‘fate’, and ‘gēn’ is ‘still, yet’, so ‘ne … þā gēn’ comes to ‘no longer’. The ‘þæt’ clause says what was no longer fated: ‘þæt hē mā mōste manna cynnes ðicgean’, ‘that he might partake of more of the kin of men’. ‘mōste’ is the past of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed’; ‘mā’ is ‘more’ with a partitive genitive, ‘manna cynnes’ (as at 712); and ‘ðicgean’, spelled with an ‘ð’, is the infinitive of ‘þicgan’, ‘take, receive, partake’, used of eating. ‘ofer þā niht’ is ‘beyond that night’: ‘ofer’ with the accusative can mean ‘during’ or ‘beyond’, and I take ‘beyond’, which is a guess about the meaning.
sentences.i: But it was no longer his fate to feast on any more of mankind after that night.

sentences.t:
Þrȳðswȳð behēold
mǣg Higelāces, hū se mānscaða
under fǣrgripum gefaran wolde.
sentences.l: Mighty-strong beheld Higelac’s kinsman how the crime-scather under sudden-grips would go on.
sentences.n: ‘Þrȳðswȳð’ is a compound of ‘þrȳð’, ‘strength’, and ‘swȳð’, ‘strong’, so ‘strong in might’; I take it as an epithet for Beowulf, in the nominative as the subject of ‘behēold’, the past of ‘behealdan’, ‘watch’, and ‘mǣg Higelāces’, ‘Higelac’s kinsman’ (the house rendering of the formula), stands in apposition. This is a guess: the word seems to occur only here, and I have no second example to confirm its form or whom it names. ‘hū se mānscaða … gefaran wolde’ is the indirect question that ‘behēold’ governs, ‘how the crime-scather meant to go on’: ‘gefaran’ is the infinitive of ‘gefaran’, ‘proceed, act’, and ‘under fǣrgripum’ is ‘under sudden grips’, a dative plural of ‘fǣrgrip’ (‘fǣr’, ‘sudden’, and ‘grip’), the way he will proceed, in the course of grabbing quickly. Beowulf lies still and watches the first victim.
sentences.i: The mighty one, Higelac’s kinsman, watched how the wicked marauder meant to go about his sudden grabbing.

sentences.t:
Nē þæt se āglǣca yldan þōhte,
ac hē gefēng hraðe forman sīðe
slǣpendne rinc, slāt unwearnum,
bāt bānlocan, blōd ēdrum dranc,
synsnǣdum swealh;
sentences.l: Not that the awesome one delay thought, but he quickly seized, at the first time, a sleeping warrior, tore him unhindered, bit the bone-locks, blood from veins drank, in huge morsels swallowed;
sentences.n: ‘Nē þæt se āglǣca yldan þōhte’ is ‘the awesome one did not think to delay’: ‘yldan’ is the infinitive of ‘ildan’, ‘delay’, and ‘þōhte’ the past of ‘þencan’, ‘think, intend’. The two opening words are not certain; the apparatus shows Grundtvig reading ‘Nō þǣr’ and Holthausen ‘Nō þæt’, and I follow Klaeber’s ‘Nē þæt’, ‘not that’. ‘ac hē gefēng hraðe forman sīðe’ is ‘but he quickly seized at the first time’: ‘gefēng’ is the past of ‘gefōn’, ‘seize’, and ‘forman sīðe’ is a dative of time, ‘at the first time’, so at the first attempt. The objects follow: ‘slǣpendne rinc’, ‘a sleeping warrior’, with the present participle of ‘slǣpan’ in the accusative masculine. ‘slāt unwearnum’ is ‘tore unhindered’: ‘slāt’ is the past of ‘slītan’, ‘tear’, and ‘unwearnum’, a dative plural of ‘un-’ with ‘wearn’, ‘hindrance, refusal’, used as an adverb; the meaning ‘irresistibly’ is a guess. ‘bāt bānlocan’ is ‘bit the bone-locks’: ‘bāt’ is the past of ‘bītan’, ‘bite’, and ‘bānlocan’ is an accusative plural of ‘bānloca’, a compound of ‘bān’, ‘bone’, and ‘loca’, ‘enclosure, lock’; I take it to mean the joints or the bony frame of the body, and I do not know the word elsewhere. ‘blōd ēdrum dranc’ is ‘drank blood from veins’: ‘ēdrum’ is a dative plural of ‘ēdre’, ‘vein’, and ‘dranc’ the past of ‘drincan’. ‘synsnǣdum swealh’ is ‘swallowed in huge morsels’: ‘swealh’ is the past of ‘swelgan’, ‘swallow’, and ‘synsnǣdum’ is a dative plural of a compound of ‘snǣd’, ‘morsel, piece’, with a prefix ‘syn-’ that I take as ‘huge, great’; it may instead be ‘syn’, ‘sin’, and so the first part is a guess.
sentences.i: The awesome one did not mean to put it off, but the first time he quickly seized a sleeping warrior, tore him without hindrance, bit into the joints of his body, drank the blood from his veins and gulped him down in great pieces;

sentences.t:
sōna hæfde
unlyfigendes eal gefeormod,
fēt ond folma.
sentences.l: at once he had of the lifeless one all consumed, feet and hands.
sentences.n: ‘sōna hæfde … gefeormod’ is ‘at once had consumed’, a perfect made from ‘habban’ and the past participle of ‘gefeormian’, ‘consume, feast on’, with the participle at the end. ‘unlyfigendes’ is a genitive singular of the present participle of ‘lifian’ with the negative prefix ‘un-’, ‘of the not-living one’, so ‘of the lifeless man’, and it depends on ‘eal’, ‘all’: ‘eal … unlyfigendes’ is ‘all of the lifeless one’. ‘fēt ond folma’ is ‘feet and hands’, naming the last pieces so that no part is left: ‘fēt’ is an accusative plural of ‘fōt’, and ‘folma’ is an accusative plural of ‘folm’, ‘hand’ (compare ‘folmum’ at 722 and ‘folme’ at 748). The unit begins in the middle of 743, after the semicolon.
sentences.i: At once he had devoured the lifeless man entire, feet and hands.

sentences.t:
Forð nēar ætstōp,
nam þā mid handa higeþīhtigne
rinc on ræste, rǣhte tōgēan[es]
fēond mid folme;
sentences.l: Forth nearer he stepped, took then with hand the stout-minded warrior on his couch, the fiend reached against him with his palm;
sentences.n: ‘Forð nēar ætstōp’ is ‘forth nearer he stepped up’: ‘nēar’ is a comparative adverb, ‘nearer’, and ‘ætstōp’ is the past of ‘ætsteppan’, ‘step up to’. ‘nam þā mid handa’ is ‘then took with his hand’: ‘nam’ is the past of ‘niman’, ‘take, seize’, and ‘handa’ is a dative singular of ‘hand’. The object is ‘higeþīhtigne rinc on ræste’, ‘the stout-minded warrior on his couch’, Beowulf: ‘higeþīhtigne’ is accusative masculine, a compound of ‘hige’, ‘mind’, and ‘þīhtig’, ‘strong, firm’, a word I have only here, so ‘stout-minded’ is my reading; ‘ræste’ is a dative singular. ‘rǣhte tōgēan[es] fēond mid folme’ is ‘the fiend reached toward him with his hand’: ‘rǣhte’ is the past of ‘rǣcan’, ‘reach’, and ‘folme’ is a dative singular, ‘with his palm’. The brackets and italics on ‘tōgēan[es]’ are Klaeber’s emendation. The manuscript has ‘on gean’, and Klaeber, with Sievers and four other editors, reads ‘tōgēanes’, ‘toward, against’; Trautmann’s reading is given in the apparatus only in the abbreviated form ‘[him] r. o.’, which I cannot expand with confidence; it appears to add ‘him’ to the line. ‘tōgēanes’ has no object in the line, so I take it as an adverb and supply ‘him’: ‘toward him’.
sentences.i: He stepped forward, nearer, and took hold with his hand of the stout-hearted man on his bed; the fiend reached out toward him with his palm;

sentences.t:
hē onfēng hraþe
inwitþancum ond wið earm gesæt.
sentences.l: he seized quickly, with hostile thoughts, and against the arm sat up.
sentences.n: The subject changes: ‘hē’ is Beowulf. ‘onfēng’ is the past of ‘onfōn’, ‘receive, seize’, and ‘hraþe’ is ‘quickly’. ‘inwitþancum’ is a dative plural, ‘with malice-thoughts’, a compound of ‘inwit’, ‘malice, treachery’, and ‘þanc’, ‘thought’; here it means ‘with hostile intent’, and the apparatus lists a proposed ‘inwitþanculum’ and Grein’s note that ‘inwitþanc’ is used as an adjective. ‘wið earm gesæt’ is ‘sat up against the arm’: ‘gesæt’ is the past of ‘gesittan’, ‘sit’, and ‘wið earm’ can be read as propped on his own arm or set against Grendel’s arm; the packet’s lines do not decide, and I give the first in the idiomatic line.
sentences.i: He quickly seized him, with hostile intent, and sat up, braced on his arm.

sentences.t:
Sōna þæt onfunde fyrena hyrde,
þæt hē ne mētte middangeardes,
eorþan scēata on elran men
mundgripe māran;
sentences.l: At once found out the keeper of crimes, that he had not met in middle-yard, of the earth’s corners, in another man a greater hand-grip;
sentences.n: ‘Sōna … onfunde fyrena hyrde’ is ‘at once the keeper of crimes found out’: ‘onfunde’ is the past of ‘onfindan’, ‘find out, discover’, and ‘fyrena hyrde’ is Grendel: ‘hyrde’ is ‘herdsman, guardian’, and ‘fyrena’ a genitive plural of ‘fyren’, ‘crime, sin’, so ‘keeper of crimes’. The ‘þæt’ clause says what he found: ‘hē ne mētte’, ‘he had not met’, the past of ‘mētan’; ‘middangeardes, eorþan scēata’ is ‘in the middle-yard, in the corners of the earth’, two genitives of place, ‘middangeardes’ singular and ‘scēata’ plural, ‘regions, corners’. ‘on elran men’ is ‘in another man’: ‘elran’ is a comparative ‘other’, and ‘men’ the dative of ‘mann’. ‘mundgripe māran’ is ‘a greater hand-grip’, the object of ‘mētte’: ‘mundgripe’ is ‘mund’, ‘hand’, and ‘gripe’, ‘grasp’, a masculine noun whose singular ends in ‘-e’ in the nominative, accusative and dative alike, so the form does not fix the case and I take the accusative that ‘mētan’ usually governs; ‘māran’ is then the accusative masculine of the weak comparative of ‘micel’. ‘scēata’ is emended. The packet’s apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘sceat/ta’, the word broken at a line end and with a doubled ‘t’; Klaeber (after E. Sc.) removes one ‘t’ and marks the vowel long. The unemended ‘sceatta’ would be a genitive plural of ‘sceatt’, ‘coin, wealth’, giving ‘the earth’s riches’, which suits the sense less.
sentences.i: At once the keeper of wickedness found out that in all the world, in all the corners of the earth, he had never met a mightier hand-grip in any other man;

sentences.t:
hē on mōde wearð
forht on ferhðe; nō þȳ ǣr fram meahte.
sentences.l: he in mind became afraid, in spirit; not by that sooner away could.
sentences.n: ‘hē on mōde wearð forht on ferhðe’ is ‘he became afraid in mind, in spirit’: ‘wearð’ is the past of ‘weorþan’, ‘become’, ‘forht’ is ‘afraid’, and ‘on mōde’ and ‘on ferhðe’ are datives, two words for the inner man (‘mōd’, ‘mind’, and ‘ferhð’, ‘spirit, life’). ‘nō þȳ ǣr fram meahte’ is ‘not for that sooner could he get away’: ‘þȳ’ is an instrumental, ‘by that’, ‘ǣr’ here a comparative adverb, ‘sooner’, and ‘meahte’ is the past of ‘magan’, ‘be able’, with ‘fram’ as an adverb, ‘away’, and no verb of motion, which Old English leaves out after such verbs. The unit starts after the semicolon in 753.
sentences.i: He grew afraid in mind and spirit, but for all that he could get away no sooner.

sentences.t:
Hyge wæs him hinfūs, wolde on heolster flēon,
sēcan dēofla gedræg;
sentences.l: His mind was hence-eager; he wished into the darkness to flee, to seek the devils’ company;
sentences.n: ‘Hyge wæs him hinfūs’ is ‘his mind was set on going hence’: ‘hyge’ is a masculine noun, ‘mind’, ‘him’ a possessive dative, and ‘hinfūs’ an adjective, ‘hin-’, ‘hence’, and ‘fūs’, ‘eager, ready’, so ‘eager to be gone’. ‘wolde on heolster flēon’ is ‘wished to flee into darkness’: ‘wolde’ is the past of ‘willan’, ‘wish’, with the infinitive ‘flēon’, and ‘heolster’ is a neuter noun, ‘hiding-place, darkness’, an accusative after ‘on’, which gives motion into it. ‘sēcan dēofla gedræg’ is ‘to seek the devils’ company’: ‘sēcan’ is an infinitive in the same chain, ‘dēofla’ a genitive plural, ‘of devils’, and ‘gedræg’ a neuter noun, ‘throng, company, tumult’. A Christian poet gives Grendel devils for company.
sentences.i: His mind was set on getting away; he wanted to flee into the darkness and seek the company of devils;

sentences.t:
ne wæs his drohtoð þǣr
swylce hē on ealderdagum ǣr gemētte.
sentences.l: not was his plight there such as he in life-days before had met.
sentences.n: ‘ne wæs his drohtoð þǣr’ is ‘his plight was not there’: ‘drohtoð’ is a masculine noun, ‘way of life, condition’, here his condition in this fight. ‘swylce hē … gemētte’ is ‘such as he had met’: ‘swylce’ is ‘such as’, and ‘gemētte’ is the past of ‘gemētan’, ‘meet, find’, so the clause compares this night with every earlier one. ‘on ealderdagum ǣr’ is ‘in life-days before’, the same compound as ‘aldordagum’ at 718, spelled differently, a dative plural.
sentences.i: His lot there was not what he had met with in his earlier days.

sentences.l: Remembered then the good one, Higelac’s kinsman, the evening-speech, up-long stood and him firmly grasped;
sentences.n: ‘Gemunde’ is the past of ‘gemunan’, ‘remember’, and takes a genitive, ‘ǣfensprǣce’, ‘the evening speech’, a compound of ‘ǣfen’, ‘evening’, and ‘sprǣc’, ‘speech’: Beowulf’s boast at 677 ff., made before he lay down, that he would meet Grendel with bare hands. ‘se gōda, mǣg Higelāces’ is ‘the good one, Higelac’s kinsman’: ‘gōda’ is the weak adjective used as a noun, and the apparatus shows that Rieger and four other editors would change it to ‘mōdga’, ‘the proud-minded one’; the manuscript has ‘goda’, and Klaeber keeps it. ‘ūplang āstōd’ is ‘stood up straight’: ‘ūplang’ is an adjective, ‘upright’, and ‘āstōd’ the past of ‘āstandan’, ‘stand up’. ‘him fæste wiðfēng’ is ‘gripped him fast’: ‘wiðfēng’ is the past of ‘wiðfōn’, ‘lay hold of’, and takes a dative, ‘him’, Grendel.
sentences.i: Then the good man, Higelac’s kinsman, remembered his evening speech, stood up straight and gripped him fast;

sentences.t:
fingras burston;
eoten wæs ūtweard, eorl furþur stōp.
sentences.l: fingers burst; the giant was outward, the earl stepped further.
sentences.n: ‘fingras burston’ is ‘fingers burst’: ‘fingras’ is a nominative plural, ‘burston’ the past plural of ‘berstan’, ‘burst, break’, and the fingers are Grendel’s in Beowulf’s grip. ‘eoten wæs ūtweard’ is ‘the giant was outward’: ‘eoten’ is a masculine noun, ‘giant’, and ‘ūtweard’ an adjective, ‘facing out’, so ‘on his way out’, the same ‘eoten’ as the ‘eotenas’ of fitt I. ‘eorl furþur stōp’ is ‘the earl stepped further’: ‘eorl’ is Beowulf, ‘furþur’ a comparative adverb, ‘further, forward’, and ‘stōp’ the past of ‘steppan’, ‘step’. The line sets the two movements against each other.
sentences.i: His fingers cracked; the giant was on his way out, and the earl stepped further forward.

sentences.l: Meant the famed one, if he could so, farther to wind away and, away from there, to flee to the fen-hollows;
sentences.n: ‘Mynte se mǣra’ is ‘the famed one meant’, with ‘mǣra’ ‘famed’ for Grendel, which I take as ironic (the poet called him a ‘famed mark-stepper’ in fitt I). The verb takes two infinitives: ‘gewindan’, ‘wind oneself away, escape’, with ‘wīdre’, ‘farther’ (an unusual form of the comparative adverb, which is usually ‘wīdor’; the apparatus shows Trautmann printing ‘wīdor’ and Sedgefield ‘wīde’), and ‘flēon’, ‘flee’. ‘(þ)ǣr hē meahte swā’ is ‘if he could so’: ‘þǣr’ can mean ‘if’ in this sense, and ‘meahte’ is the past of ‘magan’, ‘be able’. The parentheses mark a lost letter: the packet’s apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘…ær’ in one transcript and ‘hwær’ in the other, with the ‘hw’ in a different ink and crossed out later; Klaeber supplies ‘þ’, and Schücking reads ‘hwǣr’, ‘where’, so it could also be ‘wherever he could’. ‘on weg þanon’ is ‘away from there’, and ‘on fenhopu’ is ‘to the fen-hollows’: ‘fenhopu’ is an accusative plural neuter of a compound of ‘fen’ and ‘hop’, ‘retreat, hiding-place’ (compare ‘mōrhopu’ at 450, ‘moor-hollows’).
sentences.i: The famed one meant, if he could, to wrench himself farther away and flee from there to his hollows in the fen;

sentences.t:
wiste his fingra geweald
on grames grāpum.
sentences.l: he knew his fingers’ power was in the fierce one’s grips.
sentences.n: ‘wiste’ is the past of ‘witan’, ‘know’, and takes the accusative ‘his fingra geweald’, ‘the power of his fingers’, with the verb ‘to be’ left out of what follows, so ‘he knew his fingers’ power to be in …’; ‘geweald’ being a neuter noun, ‘control, rule’, and ‘fingra’ a genitive plural. ‘on grames grāpum’ is ‘in the fierce one’s grips’: ‘grames’ is a genitive singular of ‘gram’, ‘fierce, hostile’, used as a noun for Beowulf, and ‘grāpum’ a dative plural of ‘grāp’, ‘grip’, plural in form and single in sense. ‘his’ is Grendel’s.
sentences.i: He knew that the control of his fingers was in the fierce man’s grip.

sentences.t:
Þæt wæs gēocor sīð,
þæt se hearmscaþa tō Heorute ātēah!
sentences.l: That was a sad journey, that the harm-scather to Heorot went!
sentences.n: ‘Þæt wæs gēocor sīð’ is ‘that was a sad journey’: ‘gēocor’ is an adjective, ‘sad, grievous’, and ‘sīð’ is the same ‘sīð’ as at 716, ‘journey’. The manuscript has ‘he wæs’ here, and the apparatus shows Grein reading just ‘wæs’; ‘Þæt’ is Klaeber’s. ‘þæt se hearmscaþa tō Heorute ātēah’ is ‘that the harm-scather went to Heorot’: ‘hearmscaþa’ is ‘hearm’, ‘harm’, and ‘scaþa’, ‘harmer’ (see 712), ‘ātēah’ the past of ‘ātēon’, ‘draw, betake oneself’, and ‘Heorute’ a dative of ‘Heorot’. The apparatus also lists ‘þone’ (Sievers, with a query) and ‘þē’ (Cosijn, Trautmann) for ‘þæt’, which would make the clause relative, ‘the journey that the harm-scather made’; the sense is almost the same. ‘gēocor’ is said from Grendel’s side: the journey was grievous for him, and the poet’s tone is ironic.
sentences.i: It was a grievous journey that the harm-doer made to Heorot!

sentences.t:
Dryhtsele dynede; Denum eallum wearð,
ceasterbūendum, cēnra gehwylcum,
eorlum ealuscerwen.
sentences.l: The lord-hall dinned; to the Danes all came, to the fort-dwellers, to each of the bold, to the earls, an ale-dealing.
sentences.n: ‘Dryhtsele dynede’ is ‘the lord-hall dinned’: ‘dryhtsele’ is a nominative, ‘hall of the lord’s band’ (‘lord-hall’ at 485), and ‘dynede’ the past of ‘dynian’, ‘make a din, boom’. ‘Denum eallum wearð … ealuscerwen’ is ‘to all the Danes there came to be an ealuscerwen’: ‘wearð’ is the past of ‘weorþan’, ‘become’, and the datives ‘Denum eallum’, ‘ceasterbūendum’ (‘to the fort-dwellers’, from ‘ceaster’, ‘fortress’, and ‘būend’, ‘dweller’), ‘cēnra gehwylcum’ (‘to each of the bold’, with ‘cēnra’ a genitive plural) and ‘eorlum’ (‘to the earls’) are one group named four ways. ‘ealuscerwen’ is a crux. It is ‘ealu’, ‘ale’, and ‘scerwen’, a feminine noun that occurs nowhere else with certainty and is probably from ‘scirwan’, ‘deprive’, or ‘scerian’, ‘apportion’; so ‘ale-deprivation’ or ‘ale-dealing’, and either way an ironic phrase for the bitter end of a feast. The apparatus shows Kemble printing it as two words, Heyne reading ‘ealu scerpen’ (from a misreading of Andreas 1526), and Grienberger and Sedgefield ‘ealuscerpen’. I give ‘ale-dealing’ in the literal line and ‘a bitter fright’ in the idiomatic one, and the reading is disputed.
sentences.i: The lordly hall boomed; a bitter fright came upon all the Danes, the fort-dwellers, each bold man, every earl.

sentences.t:
Yrre wǣron bēgen,
rēþe renweardas.
sentences.l: Angry were both, fierce house-wardens.
sentences.n: ‘Yrre wǣron bēgen’ is ‘both were angry’: ‘yrre’ is here an adjective, ‘angry’ (it is the noun ‘anger’ at 711), ‘wǣron’ the past plural of ‘wesan’, and ‘bēgen’ the nominative of ‘both’, naming Beowulf and Grendel. ‘rēþe renweardas’ is ‘fierce ren-wardens’, in apposition: ‘rēþe’ is a nominative plural adjective, ‘fierce, cruel’, and ‘renweardas’ is a plural of ‘ren-weard’, a word found nowhere else. I take ‘ren’ as a form of ‘ærn’, ‘house’ (a spelling with the ‘r’ and vowel exchanged), so ‘house-guards’, but that is a guess: the apparatus says earlier editors took it as ‘rēn-’ from ‘regn-’, a word meaning ‘mighty’ that appears in ‘regnhearde’ at 326 (‘mightily hard’), giving ‘mighty guards’, and one editor proposes ‘rēnhearde’ (with a query). The reading is disputed.
sentences.i: Both were angry, fierce guardians of the house.

sentences.t: Reced hlynsode.
sentences.l: The hall resounded.
sentences.n: ‘reced’ is a neuter noun, ‘hall’, in the nominative, and ‘hlynsode’ the past of ‘hlynsian’, ‘resound, crash’. After ‘dynede’ at 767, the poet says the same thing again, with a different verb, as the din goes on.
sentences.i: The building rang.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs wundor micel, þæt se wīnsele
wiðhæfde heaþodēorum, þæt hē on hrūsan ne fēol,
fǣger foldbold; ac hē þæs fæste wæs
innan ond ūtan īrenbendum
searoþoncum besmiþod.
sentences.l: Then was a great wonder, that the wine-hall withstood the battle-bold ones, that it on the earth did not fall, the fair earth-building; but it was so firmly inside and out with iron-bands, with cunning-thoughts, forged.
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs wundor micel’ is ‘then it was a great wonder’, and the ‘þæt’ clauses that follow say what the wonder was. ‘wiðhæfde’ is the past of ‘wiðhabban’, ‘hold out against’, and takes a dative: ‘heaþodēorum’ is a dative plural, ‘to the battle-bold ones’, from ‘heaþo’, ‘battle’, and ‘dēor’, ‘bold’, meaning the two fighters. ‘þæt hē on hrūsan ne fēol’ is ‘that it did not fall to the earth’: ‘hē’ is ‘it’, for the masculine ‘wīnsele’ (hall), ‘hrūsan’ has the same ending in the dative and the accusative, and with a verb of falling I take ‘on hrūsan’ as ‘to the ground’, and ‘fēol’ is the past of ‘feallan’, ‘fall’. ‘fǣger foldbold’ is ‘the fair earth-building’, in apposition: ‘foldbold’ is ‘fold’, ‘earth’, and ‘bold’, ‘dwelling’, a house on earth. ‘ac hē þæs fæste wæs’ is ‘but it was so firmly’: ‘þæs’ is a genitive adverb, ‘to that degree’, and the sentence ends with ‘besmiþod’, the past participle of ‘besmiþian’, ‘make fast with smith-work’. ‘innan ond ūtan’ is ‘inside and out’, and ‘īrenbendum’ and ‘searoþoncum’ are datives plural: ‘with iron bands’ and ‘with cunning-thoughts’, from ‘searu’, ‘craft’, and ‘þanc’, ‘thought’, which together say the hall was held by iron and by skill.
sentences.i: It was a great wonder then that the wine-hall held out against the two fighters and did not fall to the ground, that fair dwelling on the earth; but it was so firmly fastened, inside and out, with iron bands, skilfully forged.

sentences.t:
Þǣr fram sylle ābēag
medubenc monig mīne gefrǣge
golde geregnad, þǣr þā graman wunnon.
sentences.l: There from the sill bent away many a mead-bench, by my hearing, adorned with gold, where the fierce ones fought.
sentences.n: ‘Þǣr fram sylle ābēag medubenc monig’ is ‘there many a mead-bench bent away from the sill’: ‘ābēag’ is the past of ‘ābūgan’, ‘bend, give way’, ‘medubenc’ a nominative, ‘mead-bench’, ‘monig’ ‘many a’ in the singular, and ‘sylle’ a dative singular of ‘syll’, ‘sill, floor-beam’. ‘mīne gefrǣge’ is ‘by my hearing’, a formula for ‘as I have heard’: ‘gefrǣge’ is a neuter noun, ‘report’, in an instrumental, and ‘mīne’ goes with it. ‘golde geregnad’ is ‘adorned with gold’: ‘geregnad’ is the past participle of ‘geregnian’, ‘adorn, set in order’, and ‘golde’ a dative of means. ‘þǣr þā graman wunnon’ is ‘where the fierce ones fought’: ‘graman’ is a nominative plural, weak, ‘the fierce ones’, and ‘wunnon’ the past plural of ‘winnan’, ‘fight’.
sentences.i: Where the fierce ones fought, many a gold-adorned mead-bench gave way from the sill, as I have heard.

sentences.t:
Þæs ne wēndon ǣr witan Scyldinga,
þæt hit ā mid gemete manna ǣnig
betlīc ond bānfāg tōbrecan meahte,
listum tōlūcan, nymþe līges fæþm
swulge on swaþule.
sentences.l: Of this did not expect before the counsellors of the Scyldings, that any of men ever by proper means splendid and bone-adorned could break up, with cunning pull apart, unless fire’s embrace should swallow it in flame.
sentences.n: ‘Þæs ne wēndon ǣr witan Scyldinga’ is ‘of this the counsellors of the Scyldings did not expect before’: ‘wēndon’ is the past plural of ‘wēnan’, ‘expect, suppose’, which takes a genitive, ‘þæs’; ‘witan’ is a nominative plural of ‘wita’, ‘wise man, counsellor’ (not the verb ‘witan’, ‘know’), and ‘Scyldinga’ a genitive plural. The ‘þæt’ clause says what: ‘þæt hit ā … manna ǣnig … tōbrecan meahte’, ‘that any of men could ever break it up’, with ‘hit’ the hall, ‘ā’, ‘ever’, and ‘tōbrecan’ an infinitive. ‘mid gemete’ is ‘by measure’, which I take as ‘in a fitting way, by ordinary means’; that is a guess. ‘betlīc ond bānfāg’ describes the hall: ‘bānfāg’ is ‘bān’, ‘bone’, and ‘fāh’, ‘adorned’, which I take as ‘adorned with bone’, perhaps antler-tips or horn on the gables, a guess. ‘betlīc’ is emended: the manuscript has ‘hetlic’, and Grundtvig reads ‘betlīc’, whose first letter Klaeber prints in italic; ‘hetlic’ would be ‘hostile, hateful’, and ‘betlīc’ I take as ‘splendid’, a guess from ‘betera’, ‘better’. ‘listum tōlūcan’ is ‘pull apart with arts’: ‘tōlūcan’ is an infinitive, ‘unlock, wrench apart’, and ‘listum’ a dative plural of ‘list’, ‘skill, cunning’. ‘nymþe līges fæþm swulge on swaþule’ is ‘unless fire’s embrace swallowed it in flame’: ‘swulge’ is a past subjunctive of ‘swelgan’, ‘swallow’, ‘fæþm’ a nominative, ‘embrace’, and ‘swaþule’ a dative; the meaning of ‘swaþul’ as ‘flame, smoke’ is a guess, and the apparatus shows editors reading ‘swolaðe’, ‘swaloðe’ and ‘staðule’.
sentences.i: The counsellors of the Scyldings had never expected that any man could break it down by ordinary means, splendid and bone-adorned as it was, or pull it apart by skill, unless the embrace of fire should swallow it in flame.

sentences.t:
Swēg ūp āstāg
nīwe geneahhe:
sentences.l: A noise up rose, new, in plenty:
sentences.n: ‘Swēg’ is a masculine noun, ‘sound, noise’, the subject of ‘āstāg’, the past of ‘āstīgan’, ‘rise’, with ‘ūp’, ‘up’. ‘nīwe geneahhe’ is two words, ‘new’ or ‘newly’ and ‘abundantly, enough’: I take ‘nīwe’ as ‘new’ and ‘geneahhe’ as an adverb of frequency or fullness, so ‘again and again’, but how the two words fit is a guess. The colon introduces what the sound did to the Danes.
sentences.i: A new sound rose up, again and again:

sentences.t:
Norð-Denum stōd
atelīc egesa, ānra gehwylcum
þāra þe of wealle wōp gehȳrdon,
gryrelēoð galan Godes andsacan,
sigelēasne sang, sār wānigean
helle hæfton.
sentences.l: To the North-Danes stood a terrible terror, to each one of those who from the wall heard the weeping, God’s adversary chant a terror-song, a victory-less song, hell’s captive bewail his pain.
sentences.n: ‘Norð-Denum stōd atelīc egesa’ is ‘to the North-Danes stood a terrible terror’: ‘Norð-Denum’ is a dative plural, ‘atelīc’ an adjective, ‘terrible’ (from ‘atol’), and ‘egesa’ a masculine noun, ‘terror’. ‘ānra gehwylcum þāra þe’ is ‘to each one of those who’, a dative with a genitive plural. ‘of wealle wōp gehȳrdon’ is ‘heard the weeping from the wall’: ‘wealle’ is a dative, ‘wōp’ an accusative, ‘weeping, outcry’, and ‘gehȳrdon’ the past plural of ‘gehȳran’, ‘hear’. Two infinitives follow ‘gehȳrdon’: ‘galan’, ‘chant, sing’, with ‘gryrelēoð’ as its object and ‘Godes andsacan’ as its subject, an accusative singular, ‘God’s adversary’ (‘andsaca’ is ‘one who opposes’; Grendel is meant); and ‘wānigean’, ‘lament’, with ‘sār’ as its object and ‘helle hæfton’ as its subject. ‘gryrelēoð’ is ‘gryre’, ‘terror’, and ‘lēoð’, ‘song’, so ‘terror-song’; whether it is a song that terrifies or a song of terror is open, and ‘sigelēasne sang’ is the same thing again, ‘a song without victory’. ‘sār wānigean’ is hard: ‘sār’ is ‘pain, wound’ and ‘wānigean’ I take as a long form of ‘wānian’, ‘lament’, which is a guess. ‘helle hæfton’ is a crux: I take ‘helle’ as a genitive, ‘of hell’, and ‘hæfton’ as ‘captive’, but the usual form would be ‘hæfta’ or ‘hæftan’; the apparatus shows Thorpe and others reading ‘helle-hæftan’ and Holthausen ‘helle hæftling’ (compare Andreas 1342, Juliana 246), all ‘captive of hell’. The sense is uncertain.
sentences.i: A dreadful terror came upon the North-Danes, every one of those who heard from the wall the outcry, God’s enemy singing his song of terror, a song without victory, hell’s captive lamenting his pain.

sentences.t:
Hēold hine fæste
sē þe manna wæs mægene strengest
on þǣm dæge þysses līfes.
sentences.l: Held him fast he who of men was in might strongest on that day of this life.
sentences.n: ‘Hēold’ is the past of ‘healdan’, ‘hold’, and ‘hine’, ‘him’, is Grendel; the subject follows as a relative clause, ‘sē þe … wæs … strengest’, ‘he who was strongest’, with ‘manna’ a partitive genitive, ‘of men’, and ‘mægene’ a dative of respect, ‘in might’ (‘mægen’, ‘might’). ‘on þǣm dæge þysses līfes’ is ‘on that day of this life’: ‘dæge’ is a dative singular, and ‘þysses līfes’ a genitive, ‘of this life’, which means ‘in this mortal life’ or ‘in those days of this world’. The sentence names Beowulf without his name and closes the fitt; Klaeber’s apparatus has a conjecture ‘[tō] fæste’ for ‘fæste’, ‘firmly’, where Conybeare and others add ‘tō’ (‘[tō] fæste’). The next fitt begins at 791.
sentences.i: He held him fast, the one who in those days was the strongest in might among men.
